title: Cultivating the Image of a Sage
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay describes a specific workplace persona: the colleague who deliberately stays quiet in most discussions, speaking only when they have something impactful to say, and cultivating an aura of wisdom in the process. Rather than framing this as shyness, the piece argues it's an intentional brand-building strategy, referencing the old E.F. Hutton advertising tagline 'When E.F. Hutton talks, people listen' as the cultural touchstone for this dynamic. It argues good leaders shouldn't tolerate the sage persona because it robs the team of everyday input, and recommends actively drawing these colleagues into ongoing dialogue through direct questions rather than letting them opt out of routine discussion.
points: Distinguishes the 'sage' persona — deliberate strategic silence to build a brand of wisdom — from genuine shyness or introversion.
Argues the sage pattern robs teams of everyday input by design, since the person only engages when it will have maximum impact.
Uses the E.F. Hutton advertising campaign as a cultural reference point for the appeal of selective, high-impact speech.
Recommends leaders actively counter the pattern by asking sages direct questions during ordinary discussion rather than waiting for their input.
Closes on the principle that personal brand-building is always subordinate to substantive team contribution.
quotes: They only enter the fray when they have something very special to say. Because what they offer is usually different and insightful, people get quiet when they speak.
Don’t be fooled. These colleagues are not shy or introverted. They intentionally choose not to say much unless their message will have a profound impact on others.
But they rob the team of their everyday input. By choosing not to engage as ideas develop, they allow the team to wander and find their way without their help.
The tagline, “When E.F. Hutton talks, people listen,” captured this idea to the delight of a generation of television consumers.
Good leaders don’t allow sages to climb the mountain. They insist on hearing what they have to say as the dialogue unfolds.
